description:
Passionate about AI/ML, mathematics, data science, and space technology.
Aim: To build a software-based solution for uncovering meaningful environmental patterns using NASA's Earth observation data. Our interests include Python, statistical modelling, machine learning, predictive analytics, geospatial analysis, & scientific visualization.
Goal: Go beyond displaying data—to discover trends, investigate Earth's changing systems, & transform scientific observations into actionable insights.
summary:
Kalyx is a full-stack web application that lets anyone investigate how the Earth is changing, without writing code or processing satellite files. A user picks an environmental variable from a catalogue (precipitation, land surface temperature, soil wetness, ozone and others), chooses a location, sets a period, and runs an analysis. KALYX then generates the time series and estimates the rate of change using linear regression and Sen’s slope. It tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test, adjusted for seasonality and autocorrelation. A pixel-level map with Benjamini-Hochberg correction shows where trends differ, including opposite trends within one region. The results come with a plain-language verdict and exportable data.

This addresses the Earth System Trend Detective challenge directly: identify variables, acquire regional data, visualize change over time, and test trends statistically.

It matters because environmental evidence is hard to reach. Many people can see a graph but cannot tell if a trend is real. KALYX makes that judgement accessible, and it warns that non-significant results are not proof of no change.
details:
What it does and how it works

KALYX is a web application for investigating environmental change. A user works through a guided workflow:

  1. Choose a variable. A catalogue lists eight Earth-system variables with their NASA source, resolution, cadence and coverage. Examples are GPM IMERG precipitation, MODIS land surface temperature, and MERRA-2 soil wetness and runoff. A search box also queries NASA's Earthdata CMR for other datasets.
    • Simulated demo series: a seeded simulation, labelled as simulated everywhere, that shows the pipeline for a point or a drawn area.
    • Imported CSV: a column picker detects the date, value and quality columns, and lets the user set a scale factor, offset, fill value and quality cutoff.
    • NASA AppEEARS: a live point fetch for MODIS land surface temperature and NDVI.
    • NASA GES DISC: a live gridded fetch for precipitation (GPM IMERG), soil wetness and runoff (MERRA-2), and evapotranspiration (GLDAS). Fetches run as background jobs with progress shown and results cached.
    • Linear regression with a 95% confidence interval, in units per decade.
    • Sen's slope as a robust second estimate of the rate of change.
    • The Mann-Kendall test, with a variance adjustment for autocorrelation measured on the detrended residuals.
    • The seasonal Mann-Kendall test, so the seasonal cycle cannot create or hide a trend.
    • A plain-language verdict, such as "Significant decreasing trend", "Increasing but not statistically significant", or "Insufficient data".
  2. Map the trend. In pixel mode, every cell inside the area is tested separately, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction controls false positives across the many tests. The cells are drawn on the satellite map, with significant cells outlined. The map flags opposite trends inside one area, which an average would hide.
  3. Export. The user can download a PDF report with the setup, finding, charts, trend map and limitations, or copy the time series as CSV and the analysis metadata as JSON.

A long Learn section explains each method in plain language, from reading the verdict to seasonality, autocorrelation, false discoveries, data quality and a step-by-step method for a good investigation.

Benefits

  • No code or file wrangling. Students and the public get a trend assessment without writing scripts or handling satellite file formats.
  • Honest statistics. The app avoids calling a trend significant just because a graph slopes. It also says that a non-significant result is not proof of no change, and that association is not causation.
  • Data transparency. Every result shows its data origin, the aggregation used, the spatial support (point or area average) and what was dropped for quality.
  • Spatial detail. It shows where a variable is changing, not only the area average.
  • Reproducible. Results state the dataset, method, significance level and number of observations, and the PDF records them.

Intended impact

The aim is to make satellite-based trend investigation something a student, teacher or interested citizen can do and understand, while teaching good statistical habits. It can also give researchers a quick first look at a region before a deeper study. It is an educational and exploratory tool, not a source of publishable findings on its own.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript and Vite. Leaflet displays NASA GIBS imagery, polygon drawing and the trend overlay. Charts are custom SVG.
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI. NumPy, SciPy, pandas and xarray handle the statistics and gridded data. Matplotlib and ReportLab build the PDF report. Requests calls the NASA services, and earthaccess with h5netcdf and dask reads GES DISC files.
  • Testing: pytest, with 22 passing tests. They cover the statistics, aggregation, CSV parsing and filtering, polygon masks and area weighting, xarray conversion and unit handling, per-cell opposite-trend detection with false-discovery control, both fetch job flows with fake connectors, CMR parsing, and PDF generation. The frontend builds without type errors.
  • NASA data and services: NASA GIBS imagery, AppEEARS, GES DISC, Earthdata CMR, and the GPM IMERG, MODIS, MERRA-2 and GLDAS products. OMI ozone and NASA Giovanni are in the catalogue but have no live connector, so they need CSV import.
  • Design: Barlow Condensed, Inter and IBM Plex Mono fonts on an obsidian-black and cyan palette inspired by aerospace web design.
  • Hardware: an ordinary laptop with a browser. No special hardware is needed.
  • Development approach: the code was completed with the side help of an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic).

Creativity

  • It joins the whole investigation in one workflow: discover, locate, ingest, clean, test, map and report, instead of only drawing a chart.
  • Statistical safeguards are a main feature: seasonality, autocorrelation, multiple testing, area weighting and visible data quality.
  • It exposes opposite trends within an area, drawing the per-cell results directly on a real NASA satellite map.
  • The visual design pairs a cinematic landing page, with video or image slots for Earth imagery, with a compact mission-control dashboard.
  • It teaches as it analyses, through plain-language verdicts and the Learn section.

Factors considered

  • Honesty about data. The simulated source is labelled everywhere, and the live connectors are described as untested against the real services.
  • Scientific validity. Seasonality, autocorrelation, multiple testing, latitude weighting, quality flags, unit conversion and short records are all handled or flagged. During testing I found and fixed an over-correction in the autocorrelation adjustment, which now uses the detrended residuals.
  • Access to NASA services. NASA APIs need login and can be slow, so there is a CSV import fallback, background jobs and caching. Credentials stay on the backend, never in the frontend.
  • Usability. The layout is responsive from phone to desktop, with visible keyboard focus, labelled controls and reduced-motion support.
  • Scope. I focused on a small number of working data products and one statistics engine, rather than many unfinished integrations.

Known limitations

  • The AppEEARS, GES DISC and CMR connectors and the GIBS layer settings follow public documentation but have not been run against the live services. Expect small fixes on first use.
  • Live gridded data covers precipitation, soil wetness, runoff and evapotranspiration only, using monthly products. AppEEARS is point sampling only.
  • The autocorrelation adjustment is simplified, and the seasonal test has no autocorrelation correction. Per-cell tests use only 10 to 25 annual values.
  • Cells are included in an area by their centre point, so cells partly inside are counted whole or not at all.
